shield_case.description: Reference BoomShield: a 1 km-wide, 30 m-thick hydrogen layer ('floating-lid' pillow) floating with its top at 20 km; aircraft fly 250 m above it (20.25 km).

architecture.value: floating lid: system mass on the top face (~2.4 kg/m2 lid), 0.1 kg/m2 floor film, soft ties K ~10 Pa/m, slack partitions

shield_case.acoustic_model_note: Acoustics simulated as a lift-closed H2 30 m slab (3-D carpets); the floating-lid detail was checked in 2-D BEM (-28.4 dB circle, -33.4 undertrack, re unshielded) and matches the slab.

caveats.value: PLdB values use the conservative rise-time proxy; paired turbulence runs say the true reduction is ~5-8 dB larger at W 1 km.
Near-track values use R_m 8 km and are still ~1.5 dB optimistic; R_m 3 km values are 2-7 dB optimistic.
Along-track joints must be sealed: a 1 m open gap every 250 m costs ~9 dB undertrack (-24.5 vs -33.7).
Stiff ties or a stiff (load-bearing) skin can make the layer nearly transparent; faces must stay soft.
Wind shifts and stretches the carpet by km to tens of km (deltas barely change); siting needs wind climatology.
Concept-level 2-D/3-D linear+nonlinear model; no hardware, no flight test; H2 fire hazard is unresolved.

everyday_refs.caveat: PLdB (Stevens perceived level of a short impulsive boom) and dBA (A-weighted level of a steady or slowly varying sound) are different scales; placing booms among dBA sounds is indicative only.

recommended_method.value: Put booms on the PL scale and use NASA's impulsive-sound analogies as the bridge (Doebler & Rathsam's 'acoustic thermometer' of familiar impulsive sounds rated in PL): ~105 PL = nearby thunder / car door slam from inside the car; ~75 PL = distant thunder / car door slam across the street. Show dBA everyday sounds on a separate, parallel axis, not as equal numbers. No published general PLdB<->dBA conversion for booms was found (published work correlates PL and A-weighted SEL but gives no fixed offset).

db_rule.value: +10 dB is heard as roughly twice as loud; a 5 dB change is noticeable

cross_sections.name: Floating-lid pillow (H2 30 m)
cross_sections.reason: Best modelled acoustics with no static load on soft elements; mass on the lid makes the floor a stable H2-over-air interface.

cross_sections.name: Touching compliant-hoop tube raft (D ~60 m)
cross_sections.reason: Matches the 60 m slab with no ties, but the hoop must be both strong (3-9 kN/m) and soft (E*t <~1e5 N/m, 3-9 % strain): not standard balloon construction.

cross_sections.name: Lens with cross-width struts
cross_sections.reason: Zero-pressure face tension ~200 kN/m needs 1 km CFRP compression struts: 9-130 kg/m2 of structure for 2-4 kg/m2 of lift.

cross_sections.name: Drop-stitch pillow (superpressure)
cross_sections.reason: The internal ties that hold it flat couple the faces 12-80x too stiffly (~1,200-2,400 Pa/m), short-circuiting the gas layer.

cross_sections.name: Vacuum / inverted balloon
cross_sections.reason: Nothing floats (structure 1.23-1.44x lift) and the rings/struts needed to hold the vacuum open are acoustic studs.

cross_sections.name: Raft with air gaps
cross_sections.reason: Air slits leak directly: a 2 m slit costs ~15 dB at the 3 km circle.

cross_sections.name: Narrow modules, 200-300 m wide
cross_sections.reason: Edge diffraction dominates: W 250 m gives only -8 to -9 dB undertrack and -3 dB at the carpet maximum, and is 0-2 dB louder than no shield beyond ~18 km.

mooring.topic: Tether drag through the jet stream
mooring.text: A 5 cm tether crossing ~8 km of 60-80 m/s jet-stream wind carries ~350-630 kN of drag, more than the whole envelope side load; tether drag likely sets station-keeping.
Sized UHMWPE tethers (6-10 cm) see ~0.6-1.0 MN of jet-stream drag each.
Illustrative 250 m module (15 m thick, 30 m/s): ~600 N/m, ~150 kN per module.
0.50 / 1.12 / 1.99 kN per metre of corridor at 20 / 30 / 40 m/s; winds at 20 km average 10-20 m/s, winter 20-30, peaks ~50.
Tethers every 2-5 km carry 2.2-5.6 MN each at 30 m/s (90-220 t each); a 4,000 km corridor needs ~800-2,000 tethers through the jet stream.
Excluded: ~67 kW per metre of corridor, ~270 GW for 4,000 km.
Solar superheat of ~20 K raises lift ~10 % every day; constant-volume pressure swing 255 / 510 / 995 Pa for 10 / 20 / 39 K, so the layer must breathe 5-10 % daily (tethers, gas shuttle or coatings).
Each pass hits the top face with 200-600 Pa (10-25x the lid's weight); 2e5-1e6 cycles over 30 years; flex-crack pinholes are the main leak driver.

4,000 km x 1 km x 30 m holds 0.74 Mt H2 (0.8 % of a year's world supply; as helium, 45 years of output) and ~5 kt TNT-equivalent per km; at 55 mbar the layer is marginal for spark ignition; needs compartments every <=250 m and leak detection.

Jet-stream wind shifts or stretches the boom carpet by km to tens of km (cut-off 35-115 km) and a crosswind moves the shadow ~2.4 km downwind; the shield's dB reduction changes by <=0.4 dB undertrack.

headline_findings.value: A 1 km-wide, 30 m hydrogen shield cuts a Concorde boom by about 34 dB under the track and about 25 dB at the loudest point of the carpet (conservative), taking it from ~98 PLdB (conservative proxy scale; ~108 raw) to ~64 PLdB under the track and at most ~73 PLdB anywhere in the computed carpet.
Width, not gas or thickness, sets the result: 250 m wide gives only -8 to -9 dB and 500 m about -21 dB undertrack, because sound diffracts around the edges.

The result holds from Mach 1.4 to 3.2: about -33 to -36 dB under the track and -21 to -29 dB at the loudest point for Concorde, Overture and the SR-71 (Boom Overture, M1.7, simulated with an estimated preset: -36.4 dB undertrack, -27.1 dB at the carpet maximum).
These are conservative: with realistic turbulence the reduction is about 5-8 dB larger, and wind barely changes it (<=0.4 dB undertrack) though it moves where the carpet lands.

Only a soft structure works: anything stiff that holds the faces apart (struts, stiff ties, drop-stitch, vacuum frames) or any open gap leaks the boom through; the floating-lid pillow is the baseline.

The hard problems are not acoustic: mooring a 1 km layer at 20 km against the jet stream (350-630 kN drag per tether, 800-2,000 tethers), a ~10 % daily lift swing, and 0.74 Mt of hydrogen next to air traffic.

Shaping (X-59, ~75 PLdB) and Boom's Mach-cutoff 'Boomless Cruise' (M1.1-1.3) work only at low Mach; a shield's niche is faster flight (Overture's Mach 1.7 and especially Mach 2+), where neither applies.
